paper.title: Taxation and the long run allocation of labor: Theory and Danish evidence
paper.code_data_availability: No data availability statement and no Statistics Denmark project reference is given. …

registers.name_in_paper: Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA)
registers.role: sample frame, treatment and outcome construction: worker-workplace links, workplace size, stayers, new hires, hourly wage rates
variables_mentioned: annual labor income (including mandatory pension fund payments)
annual hours (imputed from ATP pension payments)
number of new hires from non-employment

registers.role: robustness: employer-reported hourly wage rate accounting explicitly for overtime and part-time work, used to impute an adjusted wage rate for the full sample
variables_mentioned: hourly wage rate reported by employers

registers.name_in_paper: Mandatory pension fund ATP (basis for the hours measure in IDA)
registers.role: linkage / construction: annual hours are imputed from ATP pension fund payments

linkages: Workers and workplaces are linked and uniquely identified over time in IDA, so worker transitions in and out of a workplace can be tracked
Workers observed with both an IDA wage rate and a WSR wage rate are linked to estimate the mapping between the two wage measures

The Kleven and Kreiner (2006) effective marginal tax function for 2006 is merged onto the hourly wage grid by converting hourly wages into annual labor income using the median annual hours in the data (1660 h)

sample.universe: The full population of workers and workplaces in Denmark, 2004-2006 (IDA)
sample.unit_of_observation: Workplace (establishment) in 2005, characterised by the number of employees n_h, the number of stayers x_h in 2006 and the average hourly wage rate
selection_rules: Employed in private sector workplaces in 2005
Exclude all observations in the top percentile of the wage distribution (wage rates above DKK 714)
Drop wages below DKK 90 (approximately the sector-level minimum wage floor in 2005)
Each worker is assigned the average hourly wage rate of his workplace; workers are aggregated to workplaces
For the WSR robustness check only: drop the top and bottom one percent of IDA wages and IDA wage rates deemed of low quality by Statistics Denmark, leaving 54% of the original sample of workers
sample.n_individuals: 1.4 million workers with an observed IDA wage rate

construction_notes: The wage rate of a worker is annual labor income (including mandatory pension fund payments) divided by annual hours; hours are based on information from the mandatory pension fund ATP and do not account for overtime, with imprecise measurement of part-time hours
Each worker is associated with the workplace average hourly wage rate, which corresponds to the wage w_i of job i in the model

Effective marginal tax rates come from the empirical tax function for Denmark for 2006 of Kleven and Kreiner (2006), deflated by the growth rate in average annual labor income between 2005 and 2006; hourly wages are converted to annual income using the median annual hours in the data (1660 h), giving marginal tax rates m_1,...,m_N for hourly wages DKK 90 to DKK 714
The participation tax is m0 = 0.59 in the baseline (0.82 in a robustness check); w0 = (1 - m0)w1 = 36.9 with w1 = 90
The tax-benefit function is constructed from the marginal tax rates by choosing T0 arbitrarily, with T1 = T0 + m0w1 and T_{i+1} = T_i + m_i(w_{i+1} - w_i)

The offer distribution P_i is the distribution of firm-specific average wages for persons entering firms in 2005 from non-employment in 2004, weighting each firm's wage by the fraction of all workers hired from non-employment by that firm

Table 1 (p. 78): mean workplace size 11.0 (median 4.0, max 4141.0); mean stayers 7.7; mean wage DKK 197.6 (median 183.2, min 90.0, max 714.1); mean new hires 3.3, of which 0.6 from non-employment; 126,400 workplaces

For the adjusted-wage robustness check the WSR wage is predicted from the IDA wage by fractional polynomial regression (Stata FRACPOLY): E(w_WSR | w_IDA) = 215.7 + 37.9[(w_IDA/100)^2 - 5.1] - 13.7[(w_IDA/100)^2(ln(w_IDA/100) - 4.1)] as printed on p. 81 (the typesetting of the bracketing is ambiguous in the PDF)

claims.statement: The composite search-technology parameter alpha is estimated at 0.0098, estimated as follows: Baseline estimation: binomial maximum likelihood on the number of stayers at 126,400 private sector workplaces, with separation rate d_h = delta + lambda*s_h(1 - P_h), participation tax m0 = 0.59, bottom wage cut-off w1 = DKK 90 and q = 1 (observed job destruction treated as true job destruction).

treatment.label: Structural on-the-job search model with non-linear taxation, fitted to observed workplace separations

register_source.value: IDA (Integrated Database for Labour Market Research), Statistics Denmark: workplace size n_h in 2005, number of stayers x_h in 2006, workplace average hourly wage rate; no register variable codes are named

definition.value: The identifying variation is cross-sectional: each workplace h enters with its number of employees in 2005 (n_h), its number of stayers in 2006 (x_h) and its average hourly wage rate w_h, together with the effective marginal tax rate m(w_h) from the Kleven and Kreiner (2006) 2006 tax function (deflated to 2005 and applied to annual income = hourly wage x 1660 h) and the offer distribution P_h estimated from hires out of non-employment. Eq. (16) maps (alpha, delta, gamma) recursively into optimal search intensities lambda*s_h and hence, via Eq. (17), into the workplace separation rate d_h.

timing.value: Workplace employment is observed in a specific week of 2004, 2005 and 2006; the base year is 2005 and separations are measured over the single year 2005 to 2006

outcome.label: alpha, the composite search-technology parameter of the model (alpha = lambda^(1+1/gamma)/c0)

register_source.value: Derived from the structural model estimated on IDA (Integrated Database for Labour Market Research) data; not itself a register variable

definition.value: Composite structural parameter alpha = lambda^(1+1/gamma)/c0, combining the job offer arrival parameter lambda with the scale c0 of the isoelastic mobility cost function c(s) = c0 s^(1+1/gamma)/(1+1/gamma); it governs how strongly search effort responds to net-of-tax wage gains in Eq. (16). Estimated by maximum likelihood on workplace stayer counts.

timing.value: One-year transition: the number of 2005 employees still employed at the workplace in 2006

units.value: structural parameter of the search model (lambda^(1+1/gamma)/c0); no units stated

estimand.target_population: Workers aged 18-65 employed in private sector workplaces in Denmark in 2005 (the workers behind the 126,400 workplaces in the estimation sample), represented in the model as a single representative worker facing the Danish effective marginal tax schedule
estimand.time_horizon: Annual: separations are measured over the single year from 2005 to 2006

population.description: Workers aged 18-65 employed in private sector workplaces in Denmark in 2005, aggregated to the 126,400 workplaces at which they work (1.4 million workers with an observed IDA wage rate); workplace average hourly wage rates between DKK 90 and DKK 714
population.period: 2004-2006; base year 2005, with stayers measured from 2005 to 2006
subgroups_defined: workers older than 50 (excluded in a robustness sample)
workers with less than 1 year of work experience (excluded in a robustness check)
population.selection: Full-population IDA data restricted to workers aged 18-65 employed in private sector workplaces in 2005; observations in the top percentile of the wage distribution (above DKK 714) excluded and wages below DKK 90 dropped; workers are aggregated to workplaces, each characterised by size n_h and number of stayers x_h

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation across 126,400 Danish private sector workplaces in 2005 in the average hourly wage rate and in the share of 2005 employees still employed at the workplace in 2006, combined with the empirical Danish effective marginal tax schedule for 2006 of Kleven and Kreiner (2006) mapped onto the hourly wage grid DKK 90-714; no policy reform or quasi-experiment is used - the tax distortions are obtained by simulating the estimated structural search model

key_assumptions.assumption: Worker and firm components in wages are independent, so the workplace average wage is the firm wage component plus noise and can be used as the job wage w_i
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 3.2 and repeated as an identification caveat in the concluding remarks; no test is offered.

key_assumptions.assumption: The distribution of job opportunities P is exogenous: the job offer distribution (and the effort cost function) is independent of the worker's current job state i
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a property of the model in Section 2.1 and listed as an identification assumption in the concluding remarks.

implies_edges.from: current job state i (current wage w_i)

formal.as_written: the effort cost function c(s) and the job offer distribution P are independent of the initial state i

key_assumptions.assumption: All workers are identical, so the underlying wage (offer) distribution is the same for every individual
key_assumptions.supported_by: Acknowledged in the concluding remarks as 'the most heroic assumption of the model'; not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: The mobility (search) cost function is isoelastic, c(s) = c0 s^(1+1/gamma)/(1+1/gamma)
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed in Eq. (15) to identify the model; the estimate gamma = 1.2682 is reported but the functional form is not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Workers are indifferent between the lowest wage job and non-employment: w1 - T1 = w0 - T0, which pins down the value of leisure/home production w0 = (1 - m0)w1
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 3.2; with m0 = 0.59 and w1 = 90 it gives w0 = 36.9. Sensitivity to m0 = 0.82 and to w1 = 80/100 is reported in Table 5.

key_assumptions.assumption: Job separations arrive as a Poisson process with workplace separation rate d_h = delta + lambda*s_h(1 - P_h), so the number of stayers out of n_h employees is binomial with staying probability exp(-d_h)
key_assumptions.supported_by: The likelihood in Section 3.3 is built on this distributional assumption; it is not tested, though Fig. 3 compares the model-generated and empirical wage distributions.

formal.as_written: Pr(x_h = x | n_h, d_h) = C(n_h, x) e^{-d_h x}(1 - e^{-d_h})^{n_h - x}

key_assumptions.assumption: The wage offer distribution P is identified by the distribution of firm-specific average wages for persons entering firms in 2005 from non-employment in 2004 (such hires reveal unselected offers)
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 3.2, following Christensen et al. (2005); no test is offered.

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is restricted to workplaces whose average hourly wage lies between DKK 90 and DKK 714 (top wage percentile excluded, wages below the minimum wage floor dropped), so the wage grid w_1,...,w_N and the offer distribution are only defined on that support
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 3.2; alternative cut-offs w1 = 80 and w1 = 100 are reported in Table 5.

threats_discussed: Part of the observed job destruction may be measurement error rather than true job destruction (addressed with a data separation rate q*delta, Table 4)

Annual hours, used to construct hourly wage rates, are imputed from ATP pension payments and ignore overtime and imprecisely measured part-time hours (addressed with Wage Statistics Register wages, Table 5 column 1)
Entry and exit behaviour of students and of workers older than 50 could drive the separations used for identification (Table 5 columns 2-3)
Plant closures and downsizing generate separations that are not voluntary mobility (Table 5 column 4 and text)
The choice of the bottom wage cut-off w1 (Table 5 columns 5-6)
The level of the participation tax m0 (Table 5 column 7)
The estimated rate of non-employment (0.295) is high relative to realistic unemployment levels
robustness_checks: Alternative data job destruction multipliers q = 1, 3, 6 (Table 4)
Wage rates adjusted for overtime and part-time work using the Wage Statistics Register, imputed by fractional polynomial regression (Table 5, column 1)
Samples excluding students and excluding workers older than 50 (Table 5, columns 2-3)
Excluding closing plants, and additionally plants downsizing by 30% or more (Table 5 column 4 and text)
Alternative bottom wage cut-offs w1 = DKK 80 and w1 = DKK 100 (Table 5, columns 5-6)
Participation tax m0 = 0.82 instead of 0.59 (Table 5, column 7)
Excluding workers with less than one year of work experience (text, p. 82)
Separate estimation for men and for women (footnote 17, p. 82)
Comparing the model-generated wage distribution with the empirical one (Fig. 3)
Computing the elasticity from the linear-tax formula (12) as a cross-check on the non-linear computation (p. 80)
unresolved_confounders: Worker heterogeneity: all workers are assumed identical, so all wage variation across individuals is job (firm) variation
Voluntary moves to lower-paid jobs for non-wage reasons are not modelled
Promotions and effort-driven wage growth within firms are not accounted for
Geographical mobility, including housing transactions, is not modelled
Identification exploits only cross-sectional variation across individuals

estimator.value: Maximum likelihood: the binomial likelihood of the number of stayers x_h out of n_h employees at each workplace, with staying probability exp(-d_h) and d_h = delta + lambda*s_h(1 - P_h) implied by the structural search model (computed in Gauss)

definition.value: The identifying variation is cross-sectional: each workplace h enters with its number of employees in 2005 (n_h), its number of stayers in 2006 (x_h) and its average hourly wage rate w_h, together with the effective marginal tax rate m(w_h) from the Kleven and Kreiner (2006) 2006 tax function (deflated to 2005 and applied to annual income = hourly wage x 1660 h) and the offer distribution P_h estimated from hires out of non-employment. Eq. (16) maps (alpha, delta, gamma) recursively into optimal search intensities lambda*s_h and hence, via Eq. (17), into the workplace separation rate d_h.

key_assumptions.assumption: Worker and firm components in wages are independent, so the workplace average wage is the firm wage component plus noise and can be used as the job wage w_i
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 3.2 and repeated as an identification caveat in the concluding remarks; no test is offered.

key_assumptions.assumption: The distribution of job opportunities P is exogenous: the job offer distribution (and the effort cost function) is independent of the worker's current job state i
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a property of the model in Section 2.1 and listed as an identification assumption in the concluding remarks.

implies_edges.from: current job state i (current wage w_i)

formal.as_written: the effort cost function c(s) and the job offer distribution P are independent of the initial state i

key_assumptions.assumption: All workers are identical, so the underlying wage (offer) distribution is the same for every individual
key_assumptions.supported_by: Acknowledged in the concluding remarks as 'the most heroic assumption of the model'; not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: The mobility (search) cost function is isoelastic, c(s) = c0 s^(1+1/gamma)/(1+1/gamma)
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed in Eq. (15) to identify the model; the estimate gamma = 1.2682 is reported but the functional form is not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Workers are indifferent between the lowest wage job and non-employment: w1 - T1 = w0 - T0, which pins down the value of leisure/home production w0 = (1 - m0)w1
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 3.2; with m0 = 0.59 and w1 = 90 it gives w0 = 36.9. Sensitivity to m0 = 0.82 and to w1 = 80/100 is reported in Table 5.

key_assumptions.assumption: Job separations arrive as a Poisson process with workplace separation rate d_h = delta + lambda*s_h(1 - P_h), so the number of stayers out of n_h employees is binomial with staying probability exp(-d_h)
key_assumptions.supported_by: The likelihood in Section 3.3 is built on this distributional assumption; it is not tested, though Fig. 3 compares the model-generated and empirical wage distributions.

formal.as_written: Pr(x_h = x | n_h, d_h) = C(n_h, x) e^{-d_h x}(1 - e^{-d_h})^{n_h - x}

key_assumptions.assumption: The wage offer distribution P is identified by the distribution of firm-specific average wages for persons entering firms in 2005 from non-employment in 2004 (such hires reveal unselected offers)
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 3.2, following Christensen et al. (2005); no test is offered.

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is restricted to workplaces whose average hourly wage lies between DKK 90 and DKK 714 (top wage percentile excluded, wages below the minimum wage floor dropped), so the wage grid w_1,...,w_N and the offer distribution are only defined on that support
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 3.2; alternative cut-offs w1 = 80 and w1 = 100 are reported in Table 5.

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimated structural parameters (alpha, delta, gamma) and the job offer distribution P are invariant to the hypothetical tax reforms, so the estimated model can be re-solved under the new tax system
The participation tax m0 (and hence T0, T1 and w1) is held fixed in every reform experiment; only the marginal tax rates m_1,...,m_(N-1) along the intensive margin are changed
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 4 and footnote 11, which also explains why it is an analytical necessity.

key_assumptions.assumption: The economy is compared across long-run steady states (no discounting), so the reform effects are steady-state differences rather than transition paths
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 2: 'we only need to consider the influence of a reform on the long run, steady state outcome'.

mediators_claimed: Search effort and job mobility: lower marginal tax rates raise the net-of-tax gain from climbing the wage ladder, which raises the Poisson search intensities lambda*s_i, shifts the steady-state wage distribution g upwards and lowers non-employment
ambiguities: The paper reports no standard error, confidence interval or p-value for this simulated quantity; it states only that the confidence intervals of its further estimations are very narrow (p. 81).

evidence.how: No standard error is printed for this estimate. Table 2 reports standard errors for the baseline (alpha, delta, gamma) only; for Table 4 the paper states that 'all standard errors are very small and not reported' (p. 81), and Table 5, the Table 3 reform experiments and the figures print none.

No confidence interval and no p-value is reported anywhere for this estimate: Section 5 states that confidence intervals of the further estimations, e.g. of epsilon, are not reported although they are said to be very narrow; no hypothesis test is performed.

No control-group or pre-period mean of this quantity is printed: the outcome is a structural parameter or a model-simulated reform effect, and neither Table 1 (workplace summary statistics) nor the estimation tables report a baseline mean or standard deviation for it.
No standard deviation of this quantity is reported in the paper.
The number of workplaces used in this alternative specification is not printed; only the baseline sample size of 126,400 workplaces is given (Table 1, p. 78).

The paper does not state that the estimated structural parameters and the offer distribution are invariant to the hypothetical tax reforms; the assumption is implicit in re-solving the estimated model under the new tax system.
No transition path is computed and no horizon is attached to the reform effects: Section 2 states only that, with no discounting, the analysis needs to consider the long run steady state outcome.

key_assumptions.assumption: Worker and firm components in wages are independent, so the workplace average wage is the firm wage component plus noise and can be used as the job wage w_i
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 3.2 and repeated as an identification caveat in the concluding remarks; no test is offered.

key_assumptions.assumption: The distribution of job opportunities P is exogenous: the job offer distribution (and the effort cost function) is independent of the worker's current job state i
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a property of the model in Section 2.1 and listed as an identification assumption in the concluding remarks.

implies_edges.from: current job state i (current wage w_i)

formal.as_written: the effort cost function c(s) and the job offer distribution P are independent of the initial state i

key_assumptions.assumption: All workers are identical, so the underlying wage (offer) distribution is the same for every individual
key_assumptions.supported_by: Acknowledged in the concluding remarks as 'the most heroic assumption of the model'; not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: The mobility (search) cost function is isoelastic, c(s) = c0 s^(1+1/gamma)/(1+1/gamma)
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed in Eq. (15) to identify the model; the estimate gamma = 1.2682 is reported but the functional form is not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Workers are indifferent between the lowest wage job and non-employment: w1 - T1 = w0 - T0, which pins down the value of leisure/home production w0 = (1 - m0)w1
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 3.2; with m0 = 0.59 and w1 = 90 it gives w0 = 36.9. Sensitivity to m0 = 0.82 and to w1 = 80/100 is reported in Table 5.

key_assumptions.assumption: Job separations arrive as a Poisson process with workplace separation rate d_h = delta + lambda*s_h(1 - P_h), so the number of stayers out of n_h employees is binomial with staying probability exp(-d_h)
key_assumptions.supported_by: The likelihood in Section 3.3 is built on this distributional assumption; it is not tested, though Fig. 3 compares the model-generated and empirical wage distributions.

formal.as_written: Pr(x_h = x | n_h, d_h) = C(n_h, x) e^{-d_h x}(1 - e^{-d_h})^{n_h - x}

key_assumptions.assumption: The wage offer distribution P is identified by the distribution of firm-specific average wages for persons entering firms in 2005 from non-employment in 2004 (such hires reveal unselected offers)
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 3.2, following Christensen et al. (2005); no test is offered.

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is restricted to workplaces whose average hourly wage lies between DKK 90 and DKK 714 (top wage percentile excluded, wages below the minimum wage floor dropped), so the wage grid w_1,...,w_N and the offer distribution are only defined on that support
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 3.2; alternative cut-offs w1 = 80 and w1 = 100 are reported in Table 5.

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimated structural parameters (alpha, delta, gamma) and the job offer distribution P are invariant to the hypothetical tax reforms, so the estimated model can be re-solved under the new tax system
The participation tax m0 (and hence T0, T1 and w1) is held fixed in every reform experiment; only the marginal tax rates m_1,...,m_(N-1) along the intensive margin are changed
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 4 and footnote 11, which also explains why it is an analytical necessity.

key_assumptions.assumption: The economy is compared across long-run steady states (no discounting), so the reform effects are steady-state differences rather than transition paths
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 2: 'we only need to consider the influence of a reform on the long run, steady state outcome'.

definition.value: The identifying variation is cross-sectional: each workplace h enters with its number of employees in 2005 (n_h), its number of stayers in 2006 (x_h) and its average hourly wage rate w_h, together with the effective marginal tax rate m(w_h) from the Kleven and Kreiner (2006) 2006 tax function (deflated to 2005 and applied to annual income = hourly wage x 1660 h) and the offer distribution P_h estimated from hires out of non-employment. Eq. (16) maps (alpha, delta, gamma) recursively into optimal search intensities lambda*s_h and hence, via Eq. (17), into the workplace separation rate d_h.

timing.value: Workplace employment is observed in a specific week of 2004, 2005 and 2006; the base year is 2005 and separations are measured over the single year 2005 to 2006

outcome.label: agreement between the model-generated wage distribution g and the empirical wage distribution

register_source.value: Derived from the structural model estimated on IDA (Integrated Database for Labour Market Research) data; not itself a register variable

definition.value: Visual comparison in Fig. 3 of the earned-wage distribution g generated by the estimated structural model (Eq. 5) with the empirical distribution of workplace average wage rates in the data; no distance statistic is reported.

timing.value: Long-run steady state of the estimated model; the underlying separations are measured over 2005-2006

units.value: not stated; the figure plots two distributions over the hourly wage grid

magnitude.interpretation: Fig. 3 shows that these distributions are close to each other (p. 79)

estimand.target_population: Workers aged 18-65 employed in private sector workplaces in Denmark in 2005 (the workers behind the 126,400 workplaces in the estimation sample), represented in the model as a single representative worker facing the Danish effective marginal tax schedule

population.description: Workers aged 18-65 employed in private sector workplaces in Denmark in 2005, aggregated to the 126,400 workplaces at which they work (1.4 million workers with an observed IDA wage rate); workplace average hourly wage rates between DKK 90 and DKK 714
population.period: 2004-2006; base year 2005, with stayers measured from 2005 to 2006
subgroups_defined: workers older than 50 (excluded in a robustness sample)
workers with less than 1 year of work experience (excluded in a robustness check)
population.selection: Full-population IDA data restricted to workers aged 18-65 employed in private sector workplaces in 2005; observations in the top percentile of the wage distribution (above DKK 714) excluded and wages below DKK 90 dropped; workers are aggregated to workplaces, each characterised by size n_h and number of stayers x_h

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation across 126,400 Danish private sector workplaces in 2005 in the average hourly wage rate and in the share of 2005 employees still employed at the workplace in 2006, combined with the empirical Danish effective marginal tax schedule for 2006 of Kleven and Kreiner (2006) mapped onto the hourly wage grid DKK 90-714; no policy reform or quasi-experiment is used - the tax distortions are obtained by simulating the estimated structural search model

key_assumptions.assumption: Worker and firm components in wages are independent, so the workplace average wage is the firm wage component plus noise and can be used as the job wage w_i
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 3.2 and repeated as an identification caveat in the concluding remarks; no test is offered.

key_assumptions.assumption: The distribution of job opportunities P is exogenous: the job offer distribution (and the effort cost function) is independent of the worker's current job state i
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a property of the model in Section 2.1 and listed as an identification assumption in the concluding remarks.

implies_edges.from: current job state i (current wage w_i)

formal.as_written: the effort cost function c(s) and the job offer distribution P are independent of the initial state i

key_assumptions.assumption: All workers are identical, so the underlying wage (offer) distribution is the same for every individual
key_assumptions.supported_by: Acknowledged in the concluding remarks as 'the most heroic assumption of the model'; not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: The mobility (search) cost function is isoelastic, c(s) = c0 s^(1+1/gamma)/(1+1/gamma)
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed in Eq. (15) to identify the model; the estimate gamma = 1.2682 is reported but the functional form is not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Workers are indifferent between the lowest wage job and non-employment: w1 - T1 = w0 - T0, which pins down the value of leisure/home production w0 = (1 - m0)w1
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 3.2; with m0 = 0.59 and w1 = 90 it gives w0 = 36.9. Sensitivity to m0 = 0.82 and to w1 = 80/100 is reported in Table 5.

key_assumptions.assumption: Job separations arrive as a Poisson process with workplace separation rate d_h = delta + lambda*s_h(1 - P_h), so the number of stayers out of n_h employees is binomial with staying probability exp(-d_h)
key_assumptions.supported_by: The likelihood in Section 3.3 is built on this distributional assumption; it is not tested, though Fig. 3 compares the model-generated and empirical wage distributions.

formal.as_written: Pr(x_h = x | n_h, d_h) = C(n_h, x) e^{-d_h x}(1 - e^{-d_h})^{n_h - x}

key_assumptions.assumption: The wage offer distribution P is identified by the distribution of firm-specific average wages for persons entering firms in 2005 from non-employment in 2004 (such hires reveal unselected offers)
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 3.2, following Christensen et al. (2005); no test is offered.

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is restricted to workplaces whose average hourly wage lies between DKK 90 and DKK 714 (top wage percentile excluded, wages below the minimum wage floor dropped), so the wage grid w_1,...,w_N and the offer distribution are only defined on that support
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 3.2; alternative cut-offs w1 = 80 and w1 = 100 are reported in Table 5.

threats_discussed: Part of the observed job destruction may be measurement error rather than true job destruction (addressed with a data separation rate q*delta, Table 4)

Annual hours, used to construct hourly wage rates, are imputed from ATP pension payments and ignore overtime and imprecisely measured part-time hours (addressed with Wage Statistics Register wages, Table 5 column 1)
Entry and exit behaviour of students and of workers older than 50 could drive the separations used for identification (Table 5 columns 2-3)
Plant closures and downsizing generate separations that are not voluntary mobility (Table 5 column 4 and text)
The choice of the bottom wage cut-off w1 (Table 5 columns 5-6)
The level of the participation tax m0 (Table 5 column 7)
The estimated rate of non-employment (0.295) is high relative to realistic unemployment levels
robustness_checks: Alternative data job destruction multipliers q = 1, 3, 6 (Table 4)
Wage rates adjusted for overtime and part-time work using the Wage Statistics Register, imputed by fractional polynomial regression (Table 5, column 1)
Samples excluding students and excluding workers older than 50 (Table 5, columns 2-3)
Excluding closing plants, and additionally plants downsizing by 30% or more (Table 5 column 4 and text)
Alternative bottom wage cut-offs w1 = DKK 80 and w1 = DKK 100 (Table 5, columns 5-6)
Participation tax m0 = 0.82 instead of 0.59 (Table 5, column 7)
Excluding workers with less than one year of work experience (text, p. 82)
Separate estimation for men and for women (footnote 17, p. 82)
Comparing the model-generated wage distribution with the empirical one (Fig. 3)
Computing the elasticity from the linear-tax formula (12) as a cross-check on the non-linear computation (p. 80)
unresolved_confounders: Worker heterogeneity: all workers are assumed identical, so all wage variation across individuals is job (firm) variation
Voluntary moves to lower-paid jobs for non-wage reasons are not modelled
Promotions and effort-driven wage growth within firms are not accounted for
Geographical mobility, including housing transactions, is not modelled
Identification exploits only cross-sectional variation across individuals

estimator.value: Maximum likelihood: the binomial likelihood of the number of stayers x_h out of n_h employees at each workplace, with staying probability exp(-d_h) and d_h = delta + lambda*s_h(1 - P_h) implied by the structural search model (computed in Gauss)

estimation.specification: Baseline estimation: binomial maximum likelihood on the number of stayers at 126,400 private sector workplaces, with separation rate d_h = delta + lambda*s_h(1 - P_h), participation tax m0 = 0.59, bottom wage cut-off w1 = DKK 90 and q = 1 (observed job destruction treated as true job destruction)
estimation.weights: The offer distribution P is constructed by weighting each firm's average wage by the fraction of all workers hired from non-employment by that firm

sample_n.value: 126,400 workplaces (the workers behind them: 1.4 million with an observed IDA wage rate)

source_table.value: Figure 3 (p. 79); the value quoted in this claim is stated in the text on p. 79

ambiguities: The figure prints no numerical values and the paper reports no test statistic, so only the direction stated in the text is recorded.

evidence.annotation: Fig. 3. Calculated and empirical wage distributions.

evidence.how: No standard error is printed for this estimate. Table 2 reports standard errors for the baseline (alpha, delta, gamma) only; for Table 4 the paper states that 'all standard errors are very small and not reported' (p. 81), and Table 5, the Table 3 reform experiments and the figures print none.

No confidence interval and no p-value is reported anywhere for this estimate: Section 5 states that confidence intervals of the further estimations, e.g. of epsilon, are not reported although they are said to be very narrow; no hypothesis test is performed.

No control-group or pre-period mean of this quantity is printed: the outcome is a structural parameter or a model-simulated reform effect, and neither Table 1 (workplace summary statistics) nor the estimation tables report a baseline mean or standard deviation for it.
No standard deviation of this quantity is reported in the paper.
The figure prints no numerical values and the paper reports no statistic for this comparison; only the direction stated in the text is recorded, so there is no point estimate to transcribe.

theory_referenced: on-the-job search model of job mobility (Burdett, 1978; Christensen et al., 2005)
outcomes_examined_not_reported: Confidence intervals for epsilon and the other post-estimation quantities: stated to be very narrow but not reported (p. 81)
